newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: AKZO IN SOLAR ENERGY ROW.
newsitem.headline: AKZO IN SOLAR ENERGY ROW.

text.p: Akzo Nobel NV faces possible court action by an angry Dutch entrepreneur who claims the chemicals giant has stolen technology that makes solar energy cheap enough to compete with conventional electricity.
"I've asked my lawyer to see whether it's possible to take legal action against Akzo Nobel," said Peter van der Vleuten, managing director of Chip Market Europe.
Akzo Nobel denies any wrong-doing and says the entrepreneur has rebuffed its attempts to resolve the dispute amicably.
Van der Vleuten initiated a 22 million guilder solar energy development project in April with the support of three universities, Dutch technical research centre TNO and Akzo.
The conflict emerged last month when Akzo applied for patents for a new solar cell technology, prompting Van der Vleuten to accuse Akzo of betraying the other group members.
"The know-how was developed by the cooperative and can't be claimed by Akzo alone," Van der Vleuten said.
But Akzo said it had developed an entirely new production process and product concept that made the flexible solar cells even more competitive than the original design.
"As usual, Akzo filed for a patent on this new technology," the firm said in a statement, adding it had planned to make this know-how available to the cooperative.
Van der Vleuten, a trader in computer memory chips, came up with the idea of making flexible solar cells from plastic film rather than glass after seeing similar solar panels in the U.S.
Working with the universities he developed a proprietary technology, using a new experimental film made by Akzo Nobel.
Akzo, initially mainly interested in building up contacts in this new industry, also agreed to carry out a feasibility study for flexible solar panels to be used on roofs.
"They found out that electricity costs would remain well below ordinary electricity from the power company. Then they realised: this could be a boom market," Van der Vleuten said.
Film is not only much cheaper than glass, it weighs a fraction and is less fragile. This means it can be put on roof tops where it will easily serve the needs of one family.
Akzo decided to go it alone in the field of solar energy after Van der Vleuten declined to sell the chemicals giant a stake in his company.
Oddly, the cooperative had made no agreements about patent rights or equity stakes.
Van der Velden said he had planned to give each partner a five-percent stake in his company, while his firm alone would retain all production rights.
"I blame myself now that we didn't make any agreement between the partners earlier," he said.
Akzo said it had tried to settle the dispute amicably, but to no avail. "Up to now it wasn't possible to reach an agreement with Van der Vleuten," Akzo said.
